subject: Nans in R-hat for parameters that don't move

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Nans in R-hat for parameters that don't move
parts:
> On Apr 22, 2015, at 2:42 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> If it's a correlation matrix, that's by design. The 1 values
> on the diagonals don't move, so you get a 0/0 in the formula.
> It's been confusing users, though --- what should we do here?
> The problem is that we don't know if it's because a parameter is
> stuck because it's not sampling or stuck by design, so I'd be
> reluctant to just put it to the max value by default.

Aahhh, interesting. I think if none of the chains move and they’re all equal to the same value, we should set n_eff to #samples and R_hat to 1, by definition. If none of the chains move but they are not all equal, we should set n_eff to 0 and R_hat to infinity. Does this make sense?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Nans in R-hat for parameters that don't move
parts:
On Wednesday, April 22, 2015 at 4:25:00 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
Aahhh, interesting.  I think if none of the chains move and they’re all equal to the same value, we should set n_eff to #samples and R_hat to 1, by definition.  If none of the chains move but they are not all equal, we should set n_eff to 0 and R_hat to infinity.  Does this make sense?

I think RStan at least does all of those already, except for returning NaN for the R_hat when there is no within-chain or between-chain variation, which I like because it makes it easier to mentally filter out the constants. But I think it would be better to have the summary not report on constants in the first place.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Nans in R-hat for parameters that don't move
parts:
I guess that could happen for generated quantities that are discrete. But then I am skeptical of reporting the minimal value of R_hat and the maximal value of n_eff. It depends on whether the continuous things that the generated quantity is a function of are mixing or not.

For parameters, transformed parameters and continuous generated quantities, the constant margins are just a waste of space in the summary.

Ben

Another case where this arises is when you pin a parameter to 0 for
identifiability (e.g., multinomial logit). I agree that 1 seems a little
weird to me. 'nan' isn't much better though. Python currently reports
